summary.text: 牛 is a pictograph of an ox, emphasizing its head and horns. It names the animal and can also serve as a radical. The supplied evidence does not date the earliest surviving example or establish when other recorded uses began.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph represents the animal through a view focused on its head and horns. The paleographic account reports early oracle-bone and bronze forms depicting a frontal head with curved horns; some bronze forms also show ears, eyes, and nose. These are interpretations of the graph, not a sequence established by dated specimens.

history.text: The received Shuowen account describes horns, head, and a tail or raised-back feature. Its gloss calls 牛 a large sacrificial animal; Duan Yucai later proposes a different gloss, interpreting the word through the animal’s work and patterns. These are lexicographic interpretations, not independent proof of the graph’s origin.

The paleographic record lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and small-seal forms, but the supplied descriptions do not date individual specimens or establish the earliest securely dated example. No specific glyph image was verified for this entry, so the forms cannot be illustrated here.

牛 also appears in a reported bronze inscription as a reference to cattle and in personal names. The cited inscription’s date and context were not independently examined, so these examples do not establish the chronology of those uses.

uncertainties.text: The evidence supports a head-and-horns pictographic analysis, but does not establish the earliest surviving specimen or the dates of the listed form classes. No specific competing formation or graphic corruption is documented here.
Modern dictionary listings include figurative stubbornness, star-name, zodiac, calendar, and surname uses, but no dated evidence establishes when these arose or how they relate to the animal sense.

The supplied local data gives Mandarin niú and Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese ngjuw and Old Chinese *[ŋ]ʷə; the character-specific Unihan record could not be accessed. 牛 is not analyzed as a phonetic component, so these readings do not establish its pictographic origin.

senses.text: The pictographic account identifies the animal as the graph’s original referent, and a reported inscription uses 牛 for cattle. The evidence does not identify the earliest securely dated attestation, so this is the earliest supported sense, not a dated first occurrence.
